# True or false: Product

Strategy, discovery, roadmaps, experiments, pricing and launches. Building got cheaper; deciding what is worth building and proving it helped did not.

10 statements (Foundation 4, Standard 4, Assured 2). Decide whether each one is true or false before you open the answer. Every answer says why and links to the page that teaches it.

Prefer the terminal? From the repository root, run `python3 exercises/quiz.py --area product`.

### 1. A product strategy is complete once it has a clear vision statement.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** A vision says where you want to be. A strategy also names the target users, the problem, what the product will not do and 2 to 4 measured outcomes. Without those, nobody can use it to decline a request.

Read more: [playbook/product/product-strategy.md](../../playbook/product/product-strategy.md)

</details>

### 2. Naming the users a product is not for helps the team turn down requests that pull the product sideways.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Most early products fail by serving everyone a little. A written "not for" line lets product and sales decline the same requests for the same reason, even from a paying customer.

Read more: [playbook/product/product-strategy.md](../../playbook/product/product-strategy.md)

</details>

### 3. Asking users in an interview whether they would use a proposed feature gives reliable evidence of its value.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** People cannot predict what they will do, and they are polite about your ideas. Ask about the last time they had the problem and follow the story. Do not pitch the solution in the interview.

Read more: [playbook/product/product-discovery.md](../../playbook/product/product-discovery.md)

</details>

### 4. Interviews with a language model that plays a customer are good evidence of a user need.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** A model asked to play a customer returns the average of what it has read, politely. Use it to draft interview guides or rehearse. Evidence of a need, a price or usability comes from real users.

Read more: [playbook/product/product-discovery.md](../../playbook/product/product-discovery.md)

</details>

### 5. Dates on a roadmap shared outside the team should be given as a range with a confidence level.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Dates come from measured throughput, for example a Monte Carlo forecast. Say "85% likely by 30 June", not "due 30 June", and tell stakeholders when the 85% date moves.

Read more: [playbook/product/roadmaps-and-prioritisation.md](../../playbook/product/roadmaps-and-prioritisation.md)

</details>

### 6. Checking an A/B test every day and stopping it when the result first turns significant raises the chance of a false win.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Repeated looks give chance many opportunities to cross the line. Fix the duration and read once at the end, or set up a sequential method designed for repeated looks before launch. Stopping early for harm is always allowed.

Read more: [playbook/product/product-metrics-and-experiments.md](../../playbook/product/product-metrics-and-experiments.md)

</details>

### 7. A guardrail that shows no significant change in a small experiment proves the change caused no harm.

Level: Assured

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** A small test cannot see small harm, so "no significant change" is not proof. Give each guardrail a margin, the largest harm you would accept. It passes only when its confidence interval rules out harm bigger than the margin.

Read more: [playbook/product/product-metrics-and-experiments.md](../../playbook/product/product-metrics-and-experiments.md)

</details>

### 8. When a business product is randomised by organisation, the sample size of the experiment is the number of organisations, not the number of users.

Level: Assured

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Users in one organisation behave alike and see the same version, so they are not independent. Forty organisations of 500 users each is a test of 40. Analyse per organisation, or use a method that allows for clustering.

Read more: [playbook/product/product-metrics-and-experiments.md](../../playbook/product/product-metrics-and-experiments.md)

</details>

### 9. A feature counts as done when its code reaches production.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Deploy is not release, and release is not value. A feature is done when users get value from it. Write success and stop criteria before rollout and check the feature after 2 to 6 weeks.

Read more: [playbook/product/launch-and-adoption.md](../../playbook/product/launch-and-adoption.md)

</details>

### 10. A price should start from the value to the customer and the cost of their alternative, with cost to serve as the floor.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Cost plus a margin tells you the lowest price you can afford, not what the product is worth. The customer's alternative is often a spreadsheet, a person or doing nothing. Check the price against cost to serve so no plan loses money by accident.

Read more: [playbook/product/pricing-and-packaging.md](../../playbook/product/pricing-and-packaging.md)

</details>
